findings.summary: New PPTX export fetches every image `src` from the deck with `credentials: "include"` and no scheme/host allowlist (browser-side SSRF / confused-deputy read)
findings.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` (pptx-actions.ts:92-101) passes each `ImageElement.data.src` straight into `docsImageFetcher`, which does `fetch(resolveImageUrl(url), { credentials: "include" })` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:49-51). `resolveImageUrl` (export-utils.ts:12-18) explicitly preserves ANY absolute scheme (`http:`, `https:`, `data:`, `blob:`, `file:`) and prefixes only relative paths with the backend base — there is no allowlist. Attack: a user with write access to a shared deck (via the collaborative CRDT, or via the `PUT` document-content endpoint that this same PR documents as accepting a full `SlidesDocument` JSON for slides — packages/documentation/developers/rest-api.md:289) sets an image element's `src` to (a) `http://10.0.0.5:8080/…` or `http://localhost:…`, causing the victim's browser to issue requests into networks only the victim can reach when they hit Export ▸ PowerPoint, or (b) a relative path such as `/api/v1/workspaces/<id>/documents/<id>/content`, which `resolveImageUrl` rewrites onto the backend origin and fetches with the victim's session cookies — the response body is then embedded verbatim as a `ppt/media/` part of the file the victim downloads (index.ts:162-165), i.e. a confused-deputy read performed with the exporter's privileges rather than the deck author's. Mitigating: auth cookies are httpOnly/SameSite=lax (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:228-230), so cross-site credential leakage is blunted, and the resulting archive stays on the victim's machine unless re-shared. The PDF path (pdf-actions.ts:43) already had this shape, so the PR widens rather than introduces the surface — and the new doc comment at pptx-actions.ts:80 asserts "backend images are same-origin-fetched with cookies", which is not what the code enforces and makes the surface read as covered.

findings.summary: No size or content-type validation on bytes fetched for PPTX embedding — an attacker-chosen image URL can force an unbounded in-memory buffer
findings.evidence: `await blob.arrayBuffer()` (pptx-actions.ts:96) buffers whatever the remote server returns, once per unique src, and every buffer is retained in the zip writer until `writer.build()` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:161-167, 379). `mime: blob.type || "image/png"` accepts any declared content type; the exporter's `extFromMime` (index.ts:82-98) is a safe allowlist so there is no zip-path traversal, but nothing caps byte count or rejects non-image responses. A deck editor pointing one src at an endless response tab-crashes the exporting user (client-side DoS only, no server impact). I searched for a size guard in export-utils.ts, pptx-actions.ts, pdf-actions.ts and packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts and found none.

findings.summary: `safeFilename` (extended to `pptx` here) strips only DOS-unsafe punctuation — control characters and Unicode bidi overrides from a collaborator-controlled title reach the download filename
findings.evidence: `safeFilename` replaces only `[\\/:*?"<>|]+` (export-utils.ts:151) and is fed `title`, which for slides comes from the shared document title any collaborator can edit (slides-export-button.tsx:41-45 → `title || "presentation"`). U+202E (RTL override), other bidi controls, and C0 control characters survive and are placed into `a.download` (export-utils.ts:61-70), enabling filename-spoofing display tricks in the browser download shelf and file manager. The true extension is still appended, so this is display spoofing, not execution; browsers additionally sanitize `download` to varying degrees. This line is pre-existing; the PR touches the adjacent signature (adding `"pptx"`) and routes a third format through it.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

samples.summary: New PPTX export fetches every image `src` from the deck with `credentials: "include"` and no scheme/host allowlist (browser-side SSRF / confused-deputy read)
samples.evidence: `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` (pptx-actions.ts:92-101) passes each `ImageElement.data.src` straight into `docsImageFetcher`, which does `fetch(resolveImageUrl(url), { credentials: "include" })` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:49-51). `resolveImageUrl` (export-utils.ts:12-18) explicitly preserves ANY absolute scheme (`http:`, `https:`, `data:`, `blob:`, `file:`) and prefixes only relative paths with the backend base — there is no allowlist. Attack: a user with write access to a shared deck (via the collaborative CRDT, or via the `PUT` document-content endpoint that this same PR documents as accepting a full `SlidesDocument` JSON for slides — packages/documentation/developers/rest-api.md:289) sets an image element's `src` to (a) `http://10.0.0.5:8080/…` or `http://localhost:…`, causing the victim's browser to issue requests into networks only the victim can reach when they hit Export ▸ PowerPoint, or (b) a relative path such as `/api/v1/workspaces/<id>/documents/<id>/content`, which `resolveImageUrl` rewrites onto the backend origin and fetches with the victim's session cookies — the response body is then embedded verbatim as a `ppt/media/` part of the file the victim downloads (index.ts:162-165), i.e. a confused-deputy read performed with the exporter's privileges rather than the deck author's. Mitigating: auth cookies are httpOnly/SameSite=lax (packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:228-230), so cross-site credential leakage is blunted, and the resulting archive stays on the victim's machine unless re-shared. The PDF path (pdf-actions.ts:43) already had this shape, so the PR widens rather than introduces the surface — and the new doc comment at pptx-actions.ts:80 asserts "backend images are same-origin-fetched with cookies", which is not what the code enforces and makes the surface read as covered.

samples.summary: No size or content-type validation on bytes fetched for PPTX embedding — an attacker-chosen image URL can force an unbounded in-memory buffer
samples.evidence: `await blob.arrayBuffer()` (pptx-actions.ts:96) buffers whatever the remote server returns, once per unique src, and every buffer is retained in the zip writer until `writer.build()` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:161-167, 379). `mime: blob.type || "image/png"` accepts any declared content type; the exporter's `extFromMime` (index.ts:82-98) is a safe allowlist so there is no zip-path traversal, but nothing caps byte count or rejects non-image responses. A deck editor pointing one src at an endless response tab-crashes the exporting user (client-side DoS only, no server impact). I searched for a size guard in export-utils.ts, pptx-actions.ts, pdf-actions.ts and packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts and found none.

samples.summary: `safeFilename` (extended to `pptx` here) strips only DOS-unsafe punctuation — control characters and Unicode bidi overrides from a collaborator-controlled title reach the download filename
samples.evidence: `safeFilename` replaces only `[\\/:*?"<>|]+` (export-utils.ts:151) and is fed `title`, which for slides comes from the shared document title any collaborator can edit (slides-export-button.tsx:41-45 → `title || "presentation"`). U+202E (RTL override), other bidi controls, and C0 control characters survive and are placed into `a.download` (export-utils.ts:61-70), enabling filename-spoofing display tricks in the browser download shelf and file manager. The true extension is still appended, so this is display spoofing, not execution; browsers additionally sanitize `download` to varying degrees. This line is pre-existing; the PR touches the adjacent signature (adding `"pptx"`) and routes a third format through it.

verdict.reason: Every element of the finding checks out against the repository. pptx-actions.ts:92-101 forwards each deck image `src` into `docsImageFetcher`; export-utils.ts:46-56 fetches it with `credentials: "include"` and zero scheme/host validation; export-utils.ts:12-18 explicitly preserves any absolute scheme and rewrites bare relative paths onto the backend origin. slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:139-166 shows the fetched bytes are embedded verbatim as a ppt/media/ part. No allowlist or sanitizer exists anywhere in packages/frontend/src (grep for allowlist|sanitizeImageUrl|validateImageUrl|new URL( found nothing), and the backend does not validate slides image srcs. The confused-deputy read is concretely exploitable because backend/src/main.ts:45-47 enables CORS for the frontend origin with credentials:true, so a planted relative src such as /api/v1/workspaces/:wid/documents/:did/content is fetched with the victim's cookies and its body is readable and embedded into the downloaded file; rest-api.md:291-293 confirms PUT .../content accepts an attacker-supplied SlidesDocument that collaborators see live. SSRF/unsafe input handling is squarely in the Security lane, and pre-existence on the PDF path (pdf-actions.ts:43) is not a refutation ground.
